translation: Miho and Satsuki, perhaps because they frequently meet in their hometown, have identical expressions and ways of speaking.
Their ways of eating sweets are particularly similar they both break cookies into small pieces with their nail-polished hands before bringing them to their mouths.
I would try to remember if it's always been that way, but my memory is vague.
The slight mannerisms and gestures from the last time I saw them may have already faded away somewhere.
Miho is now married, has bought a used single-family home in her hometown, and often hosts gatherings with friends.

Despite sometimes feeling disinclined due to my part-time job the next day, I do my best to accept Miho's invitations since it's my only touchpoint with a world outside of the convenience store and a valuable opportunity to interact with women my age who lead "ordinary" lives in their thirties.
Today, Miho invited me over for tea at her place along with Yukari who brought her small child and Satsuki who is married but without kids yet.
We all contributed by bringing cakes.
At that moment, for the first time, I felt like a part of the world.
I felt as though I had been born at that moment.
It was on this day that I was truly born as a functioning part of the world.
For two weeks before the opening, we worked in pairs and practiced relentlessly with our coworkers, pretending they were customers.

We learned to make eye contact and offer a smile and a bow, put period products into paper bags, separate warm items from cold ones when packing, sanitize our hands with alcohol after handling fast food orders.
For the sake of getting used to handling cash, real money was kept in the register during practice sessions.
But receipts clearly printed with "Training," and playing shop with fellow part-time workers all dressed in the same uniform somehow made it feel like we were merely playing at shopping games.
My younger sister, who was two years my junior, was a "normal" child unlike myself.
Yet, she didn't avoid me because of this; in fact, she admired me.
When my sister got scolded by our mother over ordinary things--things that I would not be scolded for--I would approach our mother asking: "Why are you angry?"
Once the reprimand ended because of my intervention, my sister would always tell me "Thank you," as if feeling protected.
Being uninterested in sweets or toys myself, I often gave them to her.
Hence she was always following me around.
"Dad loved yakitori, so let's grill this and eat it today," When I repeated it clearly after realizing they hadn't heard me well, my mother looked stunned.
The woman next to her, another child's mother, also seemed surprised her eyes and mouth all opened wide at once.
I found her facial expression amusing but then noticed how she was staring at my hands intently.
It occurred to me that one bird would not be enough.
"Should I get more?"
As my eyes glanced towards the sparrows that were walking nearby in a small group, my now cognizant mother cried out desperately in a voice riddled with rebuke: "Keiko!"
"Let's make a grave for the little bird and bury it.
Look everyone is crying too.
Their friend has died and they must be lonely. ..
Isn't that sad?"
"Why? The bird is already dead anyway," At my question, words failed her.
I quickly put canned coffee, a cigarette, and an American hot dog into a small-sized bag.
Meanwhile, the man who had been jingling coins in his pocket suddenly reached into his breast pocket.
From this gesture, I quickly deduced that he was going to pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
Taking the canned coffee handed out by the male customer with a slight bow.
"Ah, and one of the number 5 cigarettes.
" "Certainly.
Swiftly pulling out a Marlboro Light Menthol and scanning it at the register.
"Could you please touch for age confirmation?"
Seeing his gaze shift to the showcase filled with fast food as he touches the screen, I stop my movements.
I could ask, "Would you like something else?" but when customers seem uncertain about whether to buy something or not, I've made it a rule to take a step back and wait.
At the faint sound of coins clinking, I turn around and shift my gaze towards the cash register.
People who jingle coins in their hand or pocket are often those who are quickly buying cigarettes or a newspaper and plan to leave immediately, so I am sensitive to the sound of money.
Sure enough, there was a man approaching the register with canned coffee in one hand and his other hand still stuck in his pocket.
I swiftly navigate through the store to slip behind the counter, readying myself so as not to keep our customer waiting.
Convenience stores are filled with sounds.
The chime of incoming customers, the voice of an idol promoting new products over the in-store broadcast system.
The shouts of clerks, the sound of barcode scanning.
The noise of items being placed in baskets, the crinkle sound as bread bags are clutched, and the click-clack of heels walking around inside the store.
All these sounds mix together into a symphony known as "Convenience Store Sounds" that constantly touches my eardrums.
